headline: Australian pilots pull off first-ever Antarctic winter rescue in total darkness
meta_description: An Australian aviation crew completed a daring medical evacuation from Antarctica at -43°C in complete darkness, landing on a snow runway to save a US expediti…
summary_short: In July darkness and -43°C cold, an Australian crew landed their Airbus at a remote Antarctic station to rescue a US researcher, completing an unprecedented winter evacu…
body:
On 31 July, an Australian aviation crew executed an extraordinary medical rescue at McMurdo Station in Antarctica—the first such mission ever attempted during the Southern Hemisphere's winter and in total darkness. An Airbus A319 nicknamed Snowbird 1 touched down at Phoenix Airfield on Ross Island in temperatures of minus 43 degrees Celsius, where a US expedition member was loaded onto a stretcher and safely transferred to the aircraft. After an hour on the ground, the plane continued to Christchurch in New Zealand, where the patient received medical treatment and has since recovered well. The operation succeeded despite brutal conditions that pushed aircraft capabilities to their absolute limit.

The rescue required extraordinary coordination across multiple teams. Engineers needed 24 hours to reconfigure the plane with proper medical equipment, while meteorologists tracked a snowstorm that delayed takeoff by another 12 hours. Ground crews at the station—working in minus 45 degrees and strong winds—spent six hours grading and grooming the 3-kilometre-long compacted-snow runway to make it suitable for landing. Captain Louise Robertson, one of four pilots on the flight from Hobart, called it "the most complex operation" of her 25-year flying career and seven years at Skytraders. Her husband, Rod Robertson, piloted the actual landing.

What made this rescue genuinely historic was the timing. "We completed it on the 31 July, and the first day of any sort of sunlight, which was very minimal, would be on the 1 August," Robertson explained to the BBC. The crew operated in absolute darkness, navigating by instruments alone across one of Earth's most hostile environments. Captain Al Wallach noted that "winter operations raise the complexity significantly," while Emma Campbell of the Australian Antarctic Division emphasized how the success reflected both specialist expertise and the strong partnerships that underpin Antarctic research globally.
quick_facts: First Antarctic winter rescue ever completed in total darkness
Temperatures reached -43°C during the landing at McMurdo Station
Airbus A319 spent exactly one hour on the frozen runway
Four pilots, including husband and wife, flew the mission from Hobart
